brief.head: Chains of arbitrage
brief.text: No planner sets one world price for steel, Ajay Shah said. Traders watching Singapore, Dubai and Visakhapatnam ship goods whenever prices drift apart, and the gaps close. {067-C05}

brief.head: The closet bureaucrat
brief.text: Indians accept fluctuating prices for steel and cement, yet the elite wants the rupee to stand still. Amit Varma blamed “a closet bureaucrat inside each of us”. {067-C10}

brief.head: Openness as engine
brief.text: Trade, FDI and foreign capital arrive as a package of knowledge that lifts productivity, Ajay Shah said. Every friction on cross-border dealings slows growth itself. {067-C15}

brief.head: Only for the 0.1%
brief.text: Legal routes abroad need expensive lawyers, Ajay Shah said, so only the richest can buy a Nasdaq ETF or a London flat. For everyone else, the capital account is closed. {067-C14}

brief.head: Rival currencies
brief.text: Amit Varma’s guest Larry White studied eras when rival banks issued competing currencies. Instinct says chaos; his research, Varma said, shows “it worked marvelously well”. {067-S01}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why the rupee should float
lead.head: Strong rupee, weak argument
body: Ajay Shah has a pet peeve, and this week he aired it in full: India’s fixation on whether the rupee is “strong” or “weak”.

Amit Varma recalled the rhetoric of a dozen years ago, when the party then in opposition vowed to bring the rate down from forty or fifty rupees to the dollar. Now in power, it is mocked for a rupee past eighty.
“Stronger, weaker are just ridiculous terms,” Varma said. The exchange rate is not something a state or a central bank should try to control.
Shah agreed, and spent the hour arguing that the exchange rate is the most important price of all, and that India would be better off letting it float.
## Millimetres and inches
He began with two bumper stickers. Japan trades at some 130 yen to the dollar and is, he said, “arguably one of the most successful, most wonderful countries of the whole world”.

Now swap every old rupee for ten new ones. The rate leaps from 80 to 800 to the dollar, and nothing changes. Getting excited about the level, Shah said, is like measuring his height in millimetres rather than inches. {067-C02}
What does matter is who wins and who loses. A depreciation from 80 to 90 helps exporters; an appreciation to 70 helps the Indian buying a foreign phone. Every price, Shah said, cuts both ways.
The rupee also reaches deals that never leave India. Through import parity pricing, the Indian price of steel is the London Metal Exchange price times the exchange rate.

Bigger still is finance. Vast sums slosh in and out of India as investment, and economists who think the exchange rate is about trade, Shah said, are describing a world that went away fifty years ago.
Hence the line he borrowed from Josh Felman, whom Varma called a great thinker: “The exchange rate is the most important price of all.” {067-C01}

Governments, Shah said, live in one of three rooms: North Korea, where the state is party to every currency deal; India, where private deals are tightly controlled; and the advanced economies, which stay out.

Staying out is wise, he argued, because a floating rupee steadies the economy. In bad times it falls, cheapening exports and making imports dearer; in booms it rises and cools things down. It is, in his phrase, “a shock absorber”. {067-C09}
## Stuck in the middle room

India has had a taste of the third room. Under RBI Governor Subbarao, from about 2007 to 2012 or 2013, the central bank for long stretches did no currency trading. Under Raghuram Rajan, the rupee went back to being heavily managed. {067-S07}
“So we have tasted exchange rate flexibility,” Shah said, “but unfortunately we just went back to the bad ideas.”
Varma was blunter about the controls that remain, which force ordinary people to act like criminals with their own money. “This is not merely coercion,” he said. “It is also theft.” {067-C11}
## Feeling the stones
One foundation is poured, Shah said: the RBI is now accountable for an inflation target, not for an exchange rate.

The rest must be dismantled one regulation at a time, by full-time teams who study data and persuade. India once had such a community for currency reform, Shah said. It no longer does, and so nothing moves.
lead.reelName: the case for a floating rupee

second.label: The oil shock
second.head: Price outruns the ship
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why oil was dearer before the costly crude even sailed
body: When Ajay Shah was very young, the oil producers of the Middle East, angry at losing the Yom Kippur war, quadrupled the price of crude from two dollars to eight. {067-S03}

People then asked why prices in India and California rose at once, when the ship carrying the costly crude had not yet left the Middle East. Shah remembers “screaming in laughter”. When the price of steel changes in London, he said, it changes here instantly. {#london}

Oil carries no label showing what was paid for it, Shah explained, and an ingot of steel is not stamped with the date it was bought. So when the world price moves, every barrel and ingot is repriced at once.

quote.text: The crude oil doesn’t carry a price labeled on top of it. So the moment a price changes, prices everywhere change.

third.head: A Korean price for Gujarat
body: Every day, Reliance sent one ship of benzene from its refinery at Jamnagar to an Indian buyer on the other side of the Gulf of Gujarat. Ajay Shah saw the deal while on the board of a company. {067-S02}
Seller and buyer were both Indian, and the trip was short. Yet the price, Shah said, was “the Korean price of benzene multiplied by the exchange rate”, so it changed every day.
This is import parity pricing, Shah said. Steel works the same way: the Indian price is the London Metal Exchange price times the exchange rate. {067-C04}

So when the rupee depreciates, a producer like Tata Steel, paying for Indian coal, iron ore, power and labour, earns more rupees for the same costs. It is, Shah said, “free money”, and an appreciation does the reverse.
third.caption: the daily benzene ship

p2.title: Leave the rupee alone
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s case, chapter by chapter, for an exchange rate set by the market and not the state

sections.label: The biggest price
sections.head: Shirts, phones and steel
sections.caption: the most important price
body: Ajay Shah fixed a baseline of 80 rupees to the dollar. A move to 90 is a depreciation, a move to 70 an appreciation. The question is who gains from each.

Take a white cotton shirt that a maker in Tiruppur can sell wholesale for 600 rupees. {#shirt} A foreigner pays 600 divided by the exchange rate, so a depreciation makes the shirt cheaper abroad and the exporter happier.

Now flip it. A phone made abroad costs $100: that is 8,000 rupees at 80 to the dollar and 7,000 at 70. {#phone} For the Indian buyer, or the Indian on holiday in Greece, an appreciation stretches the same income further.
“All prices cut both ways,” Shah said, “and this is the first level at which we have to think.” {067-C03}
## Finance rules

The deeper level is finance. Economists who don’t know finance, Shah said, think the exchange rate is about trade, but “that world went away fifty years ago”. Foreign direct and portfolio investment now dominate the currency market. {067-C06}

~ Amit Varma, who has heard his economics episodes dismissed as wonkery, said every aspect of our lives is shaped in unseen ways by such things. “No man,” he used to reply, “this shit has humanitarian consequences.” {067-J05}

quote.text: For everybody in the world, the local price of steel is the LME price of steel multiplied by an exchange rate.

sections.label: Gold to paper
sections.head: Nothing in it but the state
sections.caption: the end of the gold standard
body: Exchange rates cannot be discussed without money, Ajay Shah said, and in the deep past money was gold: first gold coins, then paper notes backed by gold in a vault.
It was a world of relative simplicity, he said, “and it was also a world of constant fear and mistrust”, since nobody knew if the issuer kept its promise.
Later the United States government put its might behind the rule that thirty-five dollars shall be one ounce of gold, and other currencies were linked to the dollar. {#gold}

John Maynard Keynes, trying to avert the currency chaos of the Great Depression, threw his weight behind such a fixed post-war order. Shah thinks the design was unwise, and it fell apart when Richard Nixon took the United States off gold. {067-J15}
## Money by decree

Since the collapse of Bretton Woods, currencies have been fiat money, money because a state says so. {067-C07} With no gold holding them together, the rate between pound, franc and rupee is set by supply and demand.
Governments, Shah said, are still “going through their stages of grief”. But the story is over: this is a world of floating exchange rates.
~ The first to grasp it, he said, was Milton Friedman, and for that you have to salute him.

quote.text: There is nothing in here other than the spirit of the Indian state. It is the Indian state that makes it so.

sections.label: Three rooms
sections.head: Which room is India in?
sections.caption: the three rooms in the house
body: Ajay Shah sorted the world’s currency regimes into three rooms. In the first, probably North Korea, the state is the counterparty to every currency transaction and uses violence against its people to enforce it.

In the second, private deals happen but under detailed rules, and the central bank trades on the market to control the rate. In India, Shah said, you must go through a bank, which earns a protected spread: “basically it is a tax upon the people that is being given to banks”.
Amit Varma went further. This is not merely coercion but theft, he said, because the friction burns the value of deals that would have left both sides better off. {067-C11}
## Out of the business

In the third room sit the advanced economies, which leave currencies to their people. Shah said he thought the US Fed had not traded on the currency market since 1994. {#fed} Japan, which intervenes all the time, and Switzerland, lately, are the exceptions.
For anyone trying to understand a country, Shah said, this is where to start: what is Sri Lanka doing on the exchange rate, or Pakistan, or Korea? {067-C08}
~ Varma put the question to India itself: does it want to be more like North Korea, more like the West, or is it happy chugging along as it is?

quote.text: To understand a country you must understand its exchange rate system and the exchange rate regime.

sections.label: The shock absorber
sections.head: A cushion called the rupee
sections.caption: floating rates in bad times
body: The Indian elite, Ajay Shah said, is obsessed with exchange rate stability, and he cannot see why. India is not “in a half pants anymore”: it lives with fluctuating prices for steel, cement and nickel. Why be stuck on this one?

Shah applied the general theory. Prices are “information wrapped in an incentive”, and as they move, firms and consumers reshape the resource allocation. Fixing the rupee is as silly as fixing the price of nickel.
## How the cushion works

In bad times, from floods to demonetisation to a collapse of law and order, exports suffer and the rupee depreciates. That makes exports competitive, lifts producers like Tata Steel, and makes imports dearer so buyers turn to Indian goods. {067-C09}

Capital flows push the same way. When India booms, “every dentist and grandmother in Connecticut or Kyoto” wants Indian assets and the rupee rises; on bad headlines they pull money out and it falls. {067-J07}
~ Policymakers fix the rupee, Shah argued, to win the elite’s applause. So the people to persuade are the gentle readers in the elite themselves.

quote.text: I think there’s a closet bureaucrat inside each of us who just wants a simple unchanging life.

sections.label: The India story
sections.head: A law that starts with no
sections.caption: FERA, FEMA and the lawyers
body: At independence, Ajay Shah said, India was open and flexible, but early mistakes drained the RBI’s reserves and controls followed. The British had brought in some in 1942 under wartime conditions; they intensified in the fifties. {#wartime}
Then came FERA, passed, Shah said, in 1976, “or was it 1973?” It made foreign exchange dealings a crime. Economic offences, he argued, need only a fine, say three times the ill-gotten gain.
## Banned unless permitted
FEMA replaced FERA in 1999, an opportunity Shah thinks was largely lost; criminal clauses returned in 2015. {#fema99}

The law opens by banning all cross-border activity, then lists what is allowed. Hundreds of circulars and thousands of cases have made it, in Shah’s words, “an employment guarantee program for lawyers and accountants”. {067-J08}
It is enforced by the Enforcement Directorate, whose raids go by the politer name of search and seizure. {#raids}
Shah blamed the 1991 reformers, who knew economics but not law or public administration, and gave the RBI arbitrary powers, assuming good economists would always run it. {067-C13}
~ Amit Varma saw the same error in Nehru’s generation, which assumed there would be no state overreach because good people were in charge.

quote.text: Freedom should be the norm. And maybe you have some exceptions, and we can debate what the exceptions should be.

side.boxTitle: The man who got there first
side.boxText: Ajay Shah’s recommendation was Milton Friedman’s essay *The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates*, written, he noted, in 1953. Friedman, he said, was the first to see that governments need not be in the exchange rate business. {067-R08}

contQuote.text: Our current Prime Minister has the top down thinking of Nehru and the authoritarian impulses of Indira and an ignorance of economics of both of them, frankly.

stories.start: So Ashok Desai is one of the great Indian economists
stories.end: So this is an evolution. We are somewhere on a long journey
stories.caption: Ashok Desai’s Young Turks
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a talk with Manmohan Singh’s economic adviser
stories.head: Young Turks, then and now
body: Ashok Desai, Ajay Shah said, is one of the great Indian economists. He was chief economic adviser to Manmohan Singh in 1991, and drafted the first budget speech Singh gave that July.
The two had talked a lot about exchange rates, and once Desai offered Shah a theory of generations. His own generation, he said, had woken up and questioned the socialism around international trade.

Openness to international trade was, in Desai’s words, “the single cool idea of my generation”. “We get it. We are proud that we got it,” he said, and his peers made fun of their predecessors for believing in trade barriers.
Then Desai turned to Shah. “In your generation,” he said, “the Young Turk idea is exchange rate flexibility and openness on the capital account.” {067-S06}

Shah’s generation, he went on, looked at his own with the same disbelief whenever it spoke of government policy on the exchange rate or restrictions on capital flows. Desai said he could see the look, and knew what was going on in Shah’s mind: what is wrong with this guy?
Shah drew a lesson in patience from it. “So this is an evolution,” he said. “We are somewhere on a long journey.”

~ Amit Varma returned to the anecdote later in the episode. The 1991 reformers liberalised much of the economy, he said, but not this. The exchange rate was left for the next generation, as Shah’s “beautiful anecdote” illustrates.
stories.why: Reform is a relay: each generation’s radical idea becomes the next one’s common sense. For the next leg of the journey, Shah prefers patient persuasion to sweeping change, one regulation at a time. {067-C16}

stories.caption: George Soros and the Bank of England
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Britain’s lost fight with the currency market
stories.head: Soros calls the Bank’s bluff
body: Britain, Ajay Shah said, is now among the advanced economies that have left the currency market alone. It was not always so: the Bank of England once tried to distort it. {067-S04}
George Soros, “the great man” in Shah’s telling, understood that the Bank could not keep that up, and had “the courage of his convictions to put a large bet on that market”.
His bet was that the Bank of England would fail to maintain its distortion. He won, and is reputed to have made a billion in one day.
~ Amit Varma could hardly contain himself. “It’s an incredibly famous story,” he said, “one man betting against the might of the British state.” And winning: “It’s mind blowing. I love it.”
stories.why: A central bank defending an artificial exchange rate is fighting the market, and the market can win. Such lessons are part of why, by the early nineties, the advanced economies had left exchange rates to the market.

stories.start: So there's the famous 1966 depreciation that was done by Indira Gandhi
stories.end: certain export And import changes had started taking place in the economy
stories.caption: the 1966 devaluation
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Indira Gandhi’s rupee move, judged too soon
stories.head: The slow payoff of 1966
body: For decades after independence, India’s exchange rate was fully controlled, and every change was a policy decision. The famous one, Ajay Shah said, was the 1966 depreciation done by Indira Gandhi. {067-S05}
By and large, he said, it worked extremely well. Many people misjudge it because they look only at 1967, 1968 and 1969.

Large movements in the exchange rate, he explained, play out on imports and exports with a time lag. By the oil shock of the early seventies, export and import changes had begun, and India handled the shock relatively well.
~ The lesson is to judge such moves over the right horizon: a policy that seems to do little in its first couple of years may be what saves you later.

quote.text: It sandbagged the economy in time for the oil shock of the early seventies.

stories.start: long ago, many months, I met Ajay uh by the seaside
stories.end: We can shape future generations who can hopefully uh badal the dish
stories.caption: the origin of the show
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how Everything is Everything began
stories.head: Desh badalna hai? Try YouTube
body: Months ago, Amit Varma said, he came upon Ajay Shah by the seaside, looking out at the sea, and asked him what his plan was. {067-S08}

“Desh badalna hai,” Shah said: the country must change. Varma patted him on the back and told him it would not. Shah said it again, with full stops in his voice, “maybe an exclamation mark at the end”.
After some back and forth, Varma found the answer: don’t worry, let’s do YouTube. That, he said, is the origin of the show.

~ It was the fourth of five things Varma had to tell listeners about Shah. The fifth: Shah has a cat named FEMA. Shah insists that, as a kitten, it fell from a third-floor house and broke its femur. {067-J10}
stories.why: Changing a country’s ideas, the story suggests, can begin with patient public explanation rather than policy levers. The hope, Varma said, is to shape future generations “who can hopefully badal the desh”.

quiz.q: If every old rupee were swapped for ten new ones, what would really change?
quiz.a: Nothing at all: the rate would go from 80 to 800, a change of unit.

quiz.q: How was the price of Reliance’s daily benzene shipment across the Gulf of Gujarat set?
quiz.a: The Korean price of benzene multiplied by the exchange rate, so it changed every day.

quiz.q: Whose words did Ajay Shah borrow to call the exchange rate the most important price?
quiz.a: Josh Felman’s, a great thinker in Amit Varma’s view and a past guest.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s account, what happens to a floating rupee in bad times, and why is that good?
quiz.a: It depreciates, helping exporters and import-parity producers, so it works as a shock absorber.

quiz.q: Which law replaced FERA in 1999, and how does it begin?
quiz.a: FEMA, which first bans all cross-border activity and then lists what is permitted.

quiz.q: Which two films did Amit Varma pick for Ajay Shah, who still hasn’t watched either?
quiz.a: Wim Wenders’s *Perfect Days* and Justine Triet’s *Anatomy of a Fall*, chosen months ago.
